title: A deletion filter

blocks.text: A planning service must tell planners which of a failed scenario's rules clash. Its solver can only answer "can these rules hold together?", one solve per question. Write `deletion_filter(rules, feasible)` in `filters.py`:

items: `rules` is a list of rule names; `feasible(subset)` returns `True` when the rules in `subset` can all hold together.
Return one conflict: a list of rules that cannot hold together, from which no rule can be dropped without the rest becoming feasible. Keep the rules in the order they were given.

Start with every rule kept. Then take the rules one at a time, in the order given, each exactly once: ask whether the rules kept so far, without this one, are still infeasible. If they are, drop this rule for good; if not, it stays. A rule dropped early is never asked about again, so the conflict whose rules come last in the list is the one that survives, and the caller decides which conflict is reported by ordering the rules.

When all the rules can hold together, there is no conflict: return an empty list. One call of `feasible` on the whole list before the loop is allowed for this, and the worked solution makes it; it is not one of the per-rule tests.

blocks.text: The tests replace the solver with a small oracle. About eight lines.

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Callable


def deletion_filter(rules: list[str], feasible: Callable[[list[str]], bool]) -> list[str]:
    """One irreducible conflict among `rules`, in their input order, or [] if they can all hold.

    `feasible(subset)` answers whether the rules in `subset` can hold together (one solve each).
    Each rule is tested once, in order, and left out whenever the rules kept so far stay infeasible
    without it.
    """
    if feasible(list(rules)):
        return []
    keep = list(rules)
    for name in rules:
        trial = [r for r in keep if r != name]
        if not feasible(trial):
            keep = trial
    return keep


if __name__ == "__main__":
    clash = lambda s: not {"a", "b"} <= set(s)
    print(deletion_filter(["a", "b", "c"], clash))
